This FC 27 deep dive review comes after two hundred plus hours with the game right now.

Let's address the obvious thing first, this video is late, and that's on purpose. Instead of rushing out a first impressions take in the opening week like everyone else, I wanted to actually live inside every mode long enough to know what holds up and what falls apart once the honeymoon period wears off. So let's start with gameplay, because after two hundred hours across Ultimate Team, career mode, and The Grounds, the picture is a lot clearer than it would have been on day one. On a basic level, the core engine isn't dramatically different from FC 26, but the real focus this year is manual defending, and after this much time with it, I can tell you it fundamentally changes how matches play out over a long stretch. Your defenders won't automatically win challenges anymore, and they won't make smart runs on their own either. That's been a genuine adjustment period for a lot of players I've watched and played against, good for some, frustrating for others, and after two hundred hours, that split hasn't gone away, it's actually gotten sharper. If you've put the reps in on these mechanics, the gap between you and someone who hasn't is enormous by this point in the cycle, because your opponent needs to know them too, and the AI simply isn't bailing anyone out anymore.

Let's talk about tactics next, because this is one area where my opinion has genuinely shifted the longer I've spent with it. Early on, tactics felt refreshingly simple, pick a formation, see the changes, follow the little descriptions under each option. After two hundred hours though, that simplicity holds up, it's not just a beginner-friendly surface that falls apart once you dig deeper, the system genuinely stays useful at a high level too. You can adjust your defensive line manually mid-match, and the strength and weakness markers next to each tactic actually mean something once you've tested them across enough matches to see the patterns. It did take real time to get used to, especially coming from FC 26's tactics screen, but having now built and rebuilt custom play styles dozens of times over these two hundred hours, I can say this system rewards the time investment.

Let's move into actual match gameplay, because after this many hours, the AI defending reduction is the single biggest factor shaping how every match feels. Free kicks and corners specifically have held up really well under extended use, this isn't a flashy feature that gets old after a week, it's genuinely deepened my enjoyment of dead ball situations the longer I've played. Corners work the same way, set your power, set your direction, then choose whether to make the run yourself or hold a target man up front. After two hundred hours of corners, I've got this down to a science, and it's still satisfying every single time it works. Both of these took real time to click, corners especially, but once the mechanics are second nature, which they are for me now, the results are genuinely rewarding in a way that's lasted the whole cycle rather than fading out.

Let's talk about in-game tactics too, because after months of using the quick tactics menu mid-match, this has become one of my most-used tools in the entire game. Win the ball back suddenly, flip into a counter-attacking setup instantly. Lose possession, set up for an offside trap on the fly. Across two hundred hours, the better I've gotten at adjusting this stuff live, the bigger my win rate has climbed, both in Ultimate Team and against friends. This genuinely matters more the longer you play, not less.

Let's shift over to Ultimate Team now, because this is where I've spent the overwhelming majority of those two hundred hours, it's always been my personal favorite mode, and FC 27 has kept me there consistently. The Gallery has been the standout addition, and having used it for months now rather than just the first week, I can say it's held up as a genuinely good system for pulling in new cards without needing deep pockets, which was my biggest complaint by the end of FC 26's cycle. There are some play style restrictions on specific players, and the card pool has expanded a lot since launch, enough now that I can actually speak to how the rollout has gone rather than guessing. Rewards have come steadily through objectives and SBCs without EA completely flooding the market with top tier players every week, which was genuinely my biggest worry going in. Lower divisions have stayed playable for people without a stacked squad, and that balance has held for months now, not just in the opening weeks. This is exactly why the Gallery and transfer approach has worked for me long term, it lets people who can't grind every single day still build something solid over time.

Let's talk about the actual Ultimate Team gameplay changes now, because after this many hours, the reduced AI defending has fundamentally reshaped how every single match plays out. Passing and defending both demand constant direct input now, no exceptions, no shortcuts. I lean on these mechanics heavily myself, I've defended manually for the most part since FC 26, so FC 27 has just continued rewarding that habit, and two hundred hours in, that advantage has compounded rather than evened out. The one complaint that's genuinely stuck with me the entire way through is goalkeeper movement. I spent a real chunk of those hours specifically trying to manually move my keeper, convinced for a long stretch it simply wasn't possible in this game, only to later learn from friends that it is. Even knowing that now, I still haven't been able to meaningfully work it into my game, and having played older titles where keeper movement felt tight and rewarding, both scoring and saving carried more weight because of it. It's not a dealbreaker after two hundred hours, just a persistent personal itch that's never quite gone away.

Let's talk about The Grounds now, because this is the mode where extended time has genuinely changed my read the most. Given how much demand there's been for open world games industry-wide, it made sense EA wanted in on that. But after months of returning to it periodically rather than just the launch week, the verdict hasn't improved much. The graphics still aren't there, the city still doesn't feel immersive enough to call a proper open world, and the NPCs remain lifeless. Without other online players actively around, there's still not much to actually do in it, and queuing into a match through it still mostly means standing in a square waiting for someone else to show up. Across two hundred hours, I kept checking back in hoping patches would move the needle, and some small improvements have landed, but I'm still sitting at roughly the same three to five out of ten range I would have given it in week one. The concept has potential long term, but this is the one area where extended playtime genuinely confirmed my early skepticism rather than changing it.

Let's wrap up with career mode, both manager and player career, because this is where I've put in real hours beyond just my Ultimate Team grind, and after months with it, the community reception has stayed strong the entire way, which says a lot given how often hype around a mode fades after the first few weeks. The real time transfer windows have continued to feel genuinely different and better deep into the cycle, new player faces, reworked animations, all of it has held up under extended use rather than feeling like launch-week polish that wears thin. New cutscenes and characters are still landing in updates too, so there's clearly been sustained care here rather than a one-and-done effort. Active club building and the dynamic overall system, where your form, fitness, and actual performance shift your rating over time, have both proven out properly across a full season's worth of play rather than just looking good in a trailer. Manager AI behavior has also held up well from everything I've tested across these two hundred hours. This has genuinely been the standout mode of the cycle for me, and the fact that the community sentiment hasn't soured months in says a lot.

So after two hundred plus hours, here's where I actually land. Gameplay is a genuine step forward if you've put the time into manual mechanics, and that gap only grows the longer you play. Ultimate Team's Gallery has proven itself as a real long-term system rather than a launch gimmick. The Grounds still needs real work, and extended time confirmed rather than changed that read. Career mode has been the standout of the entire cycle, consistently well received by the community months into release. This wasn't a rushed take, it's a verdict built on actually living inside this game, and I think it's a genuinely fair one.

That's pretty much my take on everything right now. Have fun out there.
